critique.good: Capability names read comfortably in two or three lines, and all plan names remain intact. The plan columns have enough space for clear, aligned availability marks.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through Business and leaves Enterprise off-screen, so readers must scroll to compare all plans. The wide table also makes it harder to keep the capability name in view while reaching the last plan.
critique.cause: The 200px capability column and the four plan columns total 495px, placing the final columns well beyond the 360px viewport.

critique.good: All plans and their availability marks are visible at once. Free and Team stay intact, and the parallel plan columns are easy to follow across each row.
critique.problems: Capability names become tall stacks of short lines, making the table difficult to scan and compare vertically. Business and Enterprise are broken inside their names.
critique.cause: The 103px capability column leaves only 82px for text. Business and Enterprise have only 44px and 57px of text space, respectively, less than their unbroken names require.

critique.good: All availability marks are visible, and the 160px capability column keeps descriptions to at most three lines. Rows have a consistent, relatively compact rhythm.
critique.problems: Every plan name breaks inside the word; Business occupies three lines. This makes the header disproportionately tall and obscures the labels needed to interpret the otherwise clear marks.
critique.cause: The 42–60px plan columns leave only 21–39px for their labels, too little to hold any of the four names intact.

critique.good: The capability names have a manageable three-line rhythm, and the plan headers remain intact. The rows are compact enough to scan across.
critique.problems: Enterprise sits almost entirely beyond the initial viewport, so readers must scroll to complete each comparison.
critique.cause: The 160px capability column preserves readable descriptions, while the intact plan headers require a total width of 455px.

critique.good: All plan names remain intact, and the narrower first column brings slightly more of Enterprise into the initial view.
critique.problems: Several capability names grow to four lines, making the table much taller while still leaving Enterprise mostly offscreen. SAML 2.0 is separated across lines.
critique.cause: Reducing the capability column from 160px to 145px crosses wrapping thresholds, but saves only 15px of horizontal overflow.

critique.good: All four availability columns are visible at once, making row-by-row comparison possible without scrolling.
critique.problems: Business and Enterprise break into awkward fragments over three lines, producing a disproportionately tall header. Capability descriptions are also lengthy, and four-hour is separated across lines.
critique.cause: Business and Enterprise receive only 53px and 56px, leaving 32px and 35px for their text. The 137px capability column also forces frequent wrapping.

critique.good: Capability names have enough room to form readable phrases, and the plan headers remain intact. The comparatively short rows make it easy to follow availability across a row.
critique.problems: Enterprise is outside the initial viewport, and Business sits at its edge. Readers must scroll to make the full plan comparison, including the Enterprise-only capabilities.
critique.cause: The 175px capability column and intact Business and Enterprise headers produce a 471px table, 111px wider than the viewport.

critique.good: More of the plan comparison is visible initially, and the capability names remain reasonably readable. The smaller overflow makes Enterprise closer at hand.
critique.problems: Business and Enterprise break inside their names, while Enterprise is still mostly outside the initial viewport. Several capability names occupy four lines, making the table taller without eliminating scrolling.
critique.cause: At 70px and 75px, Business and Enterprise have only 49px and 54px of text space. The 150px capability column also wraps descriptions more often than in r2A.

critique.good: All four plan columns and their availability marks are visible together, so readers can compare each row without scrolling. The plan columns have a steady rhythm.
critique.problems: The narrow capability column fragments descriptions into as many as five lines, making the table tall and slowing the scan down the row labels. Business and Enterprise also split inside their names.
critique.cause: The 115px capability column leaves 94px for text; the 65px Business and 66px Enterprise columns leave too little room for their headers.

understanding.purpose: Compare which subscription plans include each capability.
understanding.reading: Readers scan capability names down the first column, then compare availability across the plan columns in the same row.
groups: Free, Team, Business and Enterprise are parallel plan columns; consistent spacing helps readers compare them.
keep_intact: SAML 2.0 and four-hour as meaningful terms
may_wrap: Capability descriptions at word boundaries; their multiple lines can share the row height across all plan columns
Plan headers if a compact, no-scroll layout is preferred

bad.why: Business and Enterprise break across three lines, including isolated final letters, making the plan headers difficult to scan.
The plan headers split inside words, yet the table still requires horizontal scrolling; the long row labels also create several four-line rows.
The narrow capability column fragments descriptions across as many as five lines, while two plan names split inside words.
Two plan names split inside words and one description reaches five lines, yet the table still extends beyond the viewport.
The narrow capability column makes rows tall and descriptions choppy, while Business and Enterprise split inside words.

final.rationale: r2A gives the capability descriptions enough room to read in two or three lines and keeps all plan names intact. Its compact, consistent rows make the checkmarks easier to compare with their descriptions. The Enterprise column requires horizontal scrolling, but the initial view shows the row labels and most of the other plan columns.

general: Give descriptive row headers enough width to preserve readable phrases and make each row easy to follow across the table.
Keep short comparison-column headers intact when possible, especially when their values are simple symbols.
Judge horizontal scrolling alongside the legibility and height gained from wider columns.
specific: The capability descriptions need substantially more width than the symbol-only plan columns.
At this viewport width, fitting all five columns forces the longer plan names to split or leaves the descriptions heavily wrapped.

final.tradeoffs: r3A uses 15px less horizontal space than r2A while retaining intact headers, but one additional row becomes taller. The full-width candidates show every plan at once, at the cost of split headers and more fragmented descriptions.
final.uncertain: A designer might favor seeing all plan columns at once over preserving intact headers and shorter rows. The ranges are conservative estimates of comparable widths, not browser-tested thresholds; they should be adjusted together to preserve the preferred proportions.

A.why: The capability names wrap cleanly and the visible plan columns are easy to compare, but Enterprise sits beyond the initial viewport and requires scrolling.

B.why: The very narrow capability column breaks words throughout, making row labels difficult to read and creating exceptionally tall rows. Several headers also split.

C.why: All five plan columns are largely visible, and the row labels remain readable despite frequent wrapping. The Enterprise header extends beyond the viewport, requiring some scrolling.

D.why: The full matrix fits in the viewport and the row labels read reasonably well, but Business and Enterprise break across three lines, weakening the header hierarchy.

E.why: Capability labels wrap legibly and the visible plan headers remain intact, but Enterprise is mostly outside the initial viewport, so comparisons require scrolling.

F.why: The wider capability column gives the labels a comfortable rhythm, but the initial viewport shows only three plan columns, with Business at the edge and Enterprise requiring scrolling.

reviews.unsure: The screenshots do not show the full extent of the off-screen columns in A, E and F, so the exact scrolling distance is uncertain.

A.why: The plan headings that are visible remain intact, but the capability labels wrap over several lines and Enterprise lies mostly beyond the viewport.

B.why: The wider capability column keeps most labels readable and produces a compact table, though Enterprise is entirely offscreen and requires horizontal scrolling.

C.why: The capability column is so narrow that words break repeatedly, making the rows extremely tall and difficult to scan; two plan headings also split.

D.why: All five plan columns are largely visible and their headings remain intact, but the narrow capability column makes several rows tall and the Enterprise heading extends beyond the viewport.

E.why: All plan values fit onscreen and the capability labels remain readable, but Business and Enterprise break into three fragments, weakening the header hierarchy.

F.why: Capability labels wrap naturally and the visible plan columns are easy to compare, but Enterprise is almost entirely offscreen.

reviews.unsure: D balances readable headings and visibility of all plan values against longer capability labels; B and F are easier to read vertically but require scrolling to compare Enterprise.
